faq.q: Can diabetes cause gastroparesis even if blood sugar is controlled?

faq.a: Motilin receptors become desensitised quickly, so benefit wanes after a few days.
faq.q: Why is erythromycin used only short‑term?

exam: A 45‑year‑old diabetic woman presents with early satiety and vomiting of undigested food; scintigraphy unavailable – what is your next diagnostic step? — Perform a bedside gastric emptying test with a standardized liquid meal; if >30 % retained at 2 h, treat as gastroparesis.

Explain why metoclopramide is preferred over domperidone for a patient with HIV‑related gastroparesis in a district hospital. — Metoclopramide is oral, inexpensive, and has a dual 5‑HT4 agonist/dopamine antagonist effect; domperidone is not widely stocked and has higher cardiac risk.

A patient on chronic anticholinergic herbal remedy has worsening nausea; how does this relate to gastric motility? — Anticholinergics blunt vagal stimulation, reducing antral contractions and pyloric relaxation, leading to delayed emptying.
What red‑flag feature in a patient with suspected gastroparesis mandates urgent referral? — Persistent vomiting with aspiration pneumonia or severe electrolyte disturbance.
Distinguish between gastroparesis and a peptic stricture on endoscopy. — Gastroparesis shows a normal lumen with retained food; a stricture shows a fixed narrowing with mucosal ulceration.
Why might a patient with malaria present with delayed gastric emptying? — Severe malaria can cause autonomic dysfunction and cytokine‑mediated smooth‑muscle inhibition.

Outline the dietary advice for a patient with delayed gastric emptying when enteral feeding is not possible. — Small, frequent meals; low‑fat, low‑fiber; liquid or pureed foods; avoid large meals and carbonated drinks.
What is the rationale for avoiding high‑dose erythromycin beyond 3 days in gastroparesis? — Tachyphylaxis reduces efficacy and prolonged use increases risk of QT prolongation.
ai.title: Gastric Motility Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Gastric motility refers to the coordinated movements that mix and propel stomach contents. Impaired motility causes symptoms, malnutrition and can signal serious disease, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Vagal tone → fundic accommodation
Antral peristalsis → grinding of chyme
Pyloric relaxation → coordinated emptying
sections.p: The stomach contracts in phases (receptive, mixing, emptying) driven by the vagus nerve, enteric nervous system and hormones. Effective motility requires intact neural input, smooth‑muscle function and normal gastric outlet resistance.

b: Delayed gastric emptying = gastroparesis
Rapid emptying = dumping syndrome (post‑surgical)
Mechanical obstruction = pyloric stenosis, tumor, peptic stricture
sections.p: Motility disorders are classified by speed (delayed vs rapid) and by mechanism (neuropathic, myopathic, mechanical obstruction). In East Africa, common contributors include diabetes, HIV‑related neuropathy, post‑TB scarring, chronic malaria, and use of herbal anticholinergics.

b: Check for diabetes, HIV, recent surgery, chronic NSAID use
Look for signs of malnutrition: low BMI, muscle wasting
Assess for dehydration and electrolyte loss
sections.p: Patients present with early satiety, post‑prandial fullness, nausea, vomiting of undigested food, weight loss and sometimes abdominal pain. In severe cases, aspiration pneumonia and electrolyte disturbances can be fatal.

t.b: Is gastric emptying delayed? – >10 % retention at 4 h confirms gastroparesis
Is there a mechanical obstruction or ulcer scar? – Visual obstruction or stricture explains symptoms

t.a: Bedside gastric emptying test (fruit juice or rice water)
t.b: Does the patient retain >30 % of the test drink after 2 h? – Suggests delayed emptying when formal scan unavailable
Is diabetes present? – Hyperglycaemia worsens motility; control improves outcomes
Is HIV‑related neuropathy likely? – Low CD4 supports neuropathic cause

b: Metoclopramide 5‑HT4 agonist – improves antral contractions; avoid in Parkinson’s
Erythromycin low‑dose – motilin agonist; watch for tachyphylaxis
If obstruction present – refer for endoscopic dilation or surgery
Small, frequent meals, low‑fat, low‑fiber diet
If malnutrition severe – consider naso‑jejunal feeding
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then support gastric emptying and nutrition. Use pro‑kinetics that act on motilin receptors or dopamine antagonists; avoid drugs that further impair motility.

b: Assuming all nausea = infection – check motility history
Prescribing anticholinergics for cramps – worsens delay
Relying on normal abdominal X‑ray – may miss subtle outlet obstruction
sections.p: Confusing functional dyspepsia with true gastroparesis, overlooking medication‑induced delay, and ordering expensive tests unavailable locally.

Explain why metoclopramide is preferred over domperidone in low‑resource settings
Identify red‑flag signs that mandate urgent referral
sections.p: Examiners love scenario‑based questions that test integration of history, bedside exam, limited investigations and rational treatment.

Signs of aspiration (cough, fever, new infiltrate)
